summary: Given on the second day of a devotional festival (the Nama Ruchi Festival at the Phoenix Jagannath temple, 2019), this lecture by Indradyumna Swami glorifies the chanting of the Hare Krishna maha-mantra as the yuga-dharma, the prescribed and simplest yet most sublime process for awakening dormant love for Krishna in the age of Kali. He grounds the teaching in the famous 'harer nama' verse, explaining that we should chant humbly like a beggar begging for mercy, in the mood of the third verse of Siksastakam ('trinad api sunicena... amanina manadena'). He recounts his friendship with an advanced Gaudiya Vaishnava sadhu named Fakir Mohan, who lectured for ten years on a single verse about the holy name and spent two hours in preparatory prayers, offering arati to his beads, before chanting japa slowly and with attachment. He stresses that the goal of japa is not to 'finish rounds' but to develop taste, character and love, and that one should chant japa softly, kirtan loudly, and harinama-sankirtana at the top of one's lungs, as Haridasa Thakura did. Congregational chanting is powerful because many voices praying together, like a crowd petitioning a mayor, more surely attract the Lord's attention, and love is a two-way street in which Krishna reciprocates. Through stories of Narottama Dasa Thakura receiving prema through Mother Padmavati, Bhaktivinoda Thakura's assurance that the saints hear and reciprocate our prayers, the woodsman in the kalpavriksha forest, the three sadhus questioning Vyasadeva about the best age, and the 'footprints in the sand,' he shows that Krishna is always present as the Supersoul, more eager for our return than we are, carrying us through our difficulties. He concludes that in Kali-yuga one need only add chanting to one's life to attain perfection, because by the higher taste (param drstva nivartate) the lower tastes are given up, and urges devotees to keep chanting, avoid offenses and criticism, take shelter of the association of Vaishnavas, and say thank you to Krishna through the yajna of the holy name.
key_points: Chanting the Hare Krishna maha-mantra is the yuga-dharma and the simplest yet most sublime means of awakening love for Krishna in Kali-yuga, authorized by the 'harer nama... nasty eva gatir anyatha' verse.

One should chant humbly like a beggar begging for mercy, in the mood of Siksastakam verse 3 ('trinad api sunicena... amanina manadena'); the goal of japa is purification, good character and love for Krishna, not merely finishing rounds.

Story of the sadhu Fakir Mohan, who lectured for ten years on a single verse on the holy name and spent two hours in preparatory prayers and offering arati to his beads before chanting japa slowly, with trembling hands and tears.
Chanting grades: japa is chanted softly, kirtan loudly, and harinama-sankirtana at the top of one's lungs — as Haridasa Thakura chanted 300,000 names daily so all living entities could be delivered.

Congregational chanting is uniquely powerful: like a crowd petitioning a mayor, many devotees praying together with intensity attracts Krishna's attention, and love is a two-way street in which Krishna reciprocates (analogy of Hanuman receiving Rama's embrace).

Krishna is always present as the Supersoul, more eager for our return than we are; the 'footprints in the sand' story shows He carries us through our hardest times (one set of footprints because we are on His shoulders).

In Kali-yuga one need only add chanting to normal life; by gaining the higher taste (param drstva nivartate) the lower tastes of lust, anger and greed are given up — 'simple but not cheap' — so never stop chanting, avoid offenses/criticism, and take shelter of Vaishnava association.
references: Siksastakam verse 3 — 'trinad api sunicena taror api sahisnuna, amanina manadena kirtaniyah sada harih'; chanting humbly, more tolerant than a tree, offering respect to all.

Brhan-naradiya Purana — 'harer nama harer nama harer namaiva kevalam, kalau nasty eva nasty eva nasty eva gatir anyatha'; chanting the holy name is the only way in Kali-yuga (quoted repeatedly, 'three times' emphasis).

Srimad Bhagavatam 12.3.51 — 'kaler dosa-nidhe rajann asti hy eko mahan gunah, kirtanad eva krsnasya mukta-sangah param vrajet'; the one great virtue of Kali-yuga is that by chanting Krishna's name one attains liberation (Sukadeva to Pariksit; framed as Vyasadeva answering the three sadhus).
Bhagavad-gita 2.59 — 'param drstva nivartate'; by experiencing the higher taste one gives up the lower (hot-air-balloon / sandbags analogy).
Bhagavad-gita 4.11 — 'ye yatha mam prapadyante tams tathaiva bhajamy aham'; as all surrender to Krishna, He reciprocates accordingly ('love is a two-way street').
Bhagavad-gita 4.8 — 'paritranaya sadhunam vinasaya ca duskrtam'; the Lord descends to protect devotees, vanquish miscreants and reestablish religious principles.
Bhagavad-gita 18.70 — one who studies the Gita worships the Lord by his intelligence (paraphrased as 'he worships me by his intelligence').

Sri Bhagavata (Padyavali / Rupa Goswami) — 'krsna-varnam tvisakrsnam sangopangastra-parsadam, yajnaih sankirtana-prayair yajanti hi su-medhasah'; intelligent people worship Caitanya Mahaprabhu through sankirtana-yajna.

Brahma-samhita 5.29 (Nama-cintamani / 'cintamani-prakara-sadmasu...') — paraphrased 'nama cintamani krsnas caitanya-rasa-vigrahah'; the name is a transcendental touchstone, non-different from Krishna.

Srimad Bhagavatam Canto 7 — Prahlada Maharaja preaching to his schoolmates that Krishna consciousness (bhagavata-dharma) should begin in childhood; also the appearance of Nrsimhadeva to deliver Prahlada.

Srimad Bhagavatam 1.2.6 area / First Canto — the nine processes of devotional service 'sravanam kirtanam visnoh smaranam pada-sevanam, arcanam vandanam dasyam sakhyam atma-nivedanam' culminating in atma-nivedanam (full surrender).
Bhagavata reference to laziness/procrastination as a symptom of Kali-yuga (First Canto), cited to urge not delaying spiritual life.
Matthew 6:6 (Bible) — Jesus' instruction to go to your room, close the door and pray to your Father in private, cited alongside the need to chant in a solitary place.
stories: Fakir Mohan the sadhu — an advanced Gaudiya Vaishnava who lectured ten years on a single verse and spent two hours in prayers, offering arati to his beads, before chanting japa slowly with trembling hands and tears.
Narottama and Mother Padmavati — Mahaprabhu left prema with the personified Padma river to give the young boy Narottama, who bathed there and went mad with love of God.
Woodsman in the kalpavriksha forest — his idle wishes all came true in the desire-tree forest, including his fear that a tiger would come and eat him.
Crowd petitioning the mayor — one lone voice at the town hall goes unheard, but thousands chanting together get the roads paved; so with congregational chanting.
Three sadhus and Vyasadeva — arguing which yuga is best, they faint at the very word 'Kali,' and Vyasadeva answers that Kali-yuga is best because one need only chant.
Hot-air balloon sandbags — the balloon rises not by pushing but by dropping the sandbags, as the higher taste lets us drop the lower tastes.
Footprints in the sand — a devotee sees only one set of footprints in his hardest times because Krishna was carrying him on His shoulders.
Hanuman's embrace — offered any boon for his service, Hanuman asks only for a hug from Rama, showing love reciprocated according to one's bhakti.
quotes: It's simple, but it's not cheap.
You may not know Krishna, but he knows you very well.
Krishna's more eager that you come home than you are right now.
When you're chanting Hare Krishna, Krishna is dancing on the tip of your tongue.
Better to be moving slowly in the right direction than running hell-bent for leather in the wrong direction.

the nectar of divine love, likened to the water of Radha-kunda
